Keep your battery on a smart trickle charger or remove it entirely—dead batteries are the top reason bikes won't start after winter
Deep clean and apply corrosion protection like ACF-50 before storage, as road salt and grime hold moisture against metal causing rust
Get wheels off the ground using paddock stands to prevent tyre flat spots developing over months of static weight
Change oil before storage rather than after—fresh oil protects internal engine surfaces from acidic contaminants in used oil

faq.q: Should I start my motorcycle during winter storage?
faq.a: No, avoid short starts during storage. Brief runs without fully warming the engine cause condensation in the exhaust and oil system without burning it off, causing more harm than good. Either take it for a proper 20-minute ride or leave it completely alone.

faq.q: How long can I store a motorcycle with fuel in the tank?
faq.a: With a full tank and quality fuel stabiliser, you can safely store modern petrol for 3-4 months. Always fill the tank completely to minimise air space and prevent internal condensation that causes rust.

faq.q: Do I need to change the oil before or after winter storage?
faq.a: Change oil before storage. Used oil contains acids and combustion contaminants that can corrode internal engine surfaces over months. Fresh oil provides clean, protective lubrication throughout winter.

faq.q: Can I store my motorcycle outside in UK winter?
faq.a: Yes, but it requires extra care. Use a breathable weatherproof cover, ideally elevate it on level ground, apply extensive corrosion protection, and check it weekly. Indoor storage in a garage or unit is far better for preventing weather and salt damage.

faq.q: What should I do with my motorcycle battery during winter storage?
faq.a: Either remove the battery and keep it indoors on a monthly trickle charge, or leave it installed connected to a smart charger. Never let it fully discharge as this causes permanent damage, especially in cold temperatures.

faq.q: How do I prevent tyre flat spots during storage?
faq.a: Best option is using paddock stands to lift both wheels off the ground. Alternatively, over-inflate tyres by 5-10 psi and rotate the bike's position every few weeks to prevent prolonged pressure on one spot.

Your Complete Winter Motorcycle Storage Guide for the UK

Right then, let's talk about something most of us would rather avoid: putting the bike away for winter. I get it—after brilliant rides up to the Highlands on the NC500 or through the Peaks, the last thing you want is to cover up your machine for months. But here's the thing: I've seen too many mates fire up their bikes in March only to find corrosion, flat batteries, and seized components that could've been avoided with an hour's work in November.

I'm not saying you have to store your bike every winter—I ride year-round when I can—but if you're planning to tuck it away during the worst months, doing it properly will save you money, hassle, and that sinking feeling when your pride and joy won't start come spring.

When to Consider Winter Storage

Let's be honest about British winters. If you're down south, you might get away with riding most days. But if you're up in Scotland or the North, or if your bike's your summer tourer rather than your daily hack, there's a good case for proper storage between December and March.

I've ridden through February sleet on the A537 Cat and Fiddle, and while it's doable, it's not exactly enjoyable. More importantly, the combination of road salt, damp, and freezing temperatures absolutely batters a bike that's just sitting outside under a cover. If you know your bike's going to stand for more than a fortnight during the salt season, it's worth doing storage properly.

Finding the Right Storage Space

First job: where's your bike going to live? I've stored bikes in garages, sheds, and even shared storage units. Here's what I've learned:

Your Own Garage or Shed

Best option if you've got it. Keeps the bike dry, accessible, and lets you check on it whenever you fancy. Make sure it's properly secured—bike theft doesn't take a winter break. I use a ground anchor and chain even in my own garage.

Top tip: if your garage gets damp (most British ones do), don't seal the bike in completely. Air circulation is your friend. Moisture trapped under a cover in a cold, damp garage will cause more corrosion than leaving it uncovered in a dry space.

Professional Storage Units

If you haven't got space at home, motorcycle storage facilities are worth considering. Expect to pay £20-50 per month depending on location and security level. Look for heated units if your budget allows—they're brilliant for preventing condensation issues.

Outdoor Storage

Not ideal, but sometimes it's all we've got. If you're storing outside, invest in a proper weatherproof cover and if possible, get the bike off the ground or at least on a level, well-drained surface. I stored a Tiger outside one winter in Yorkshire—it survived, but only because I checked it weekly and followed every other step in this guide religiously.

The Pre-Storage Deep Clean

This isn't about vanity—it's about preservation. Road salt, mud, and grime hold moisture against metal surfaces, and that means corrosion. I learned this the hard way after storing a bike "just a bit muddy" one year. Come spring, I had surface rust on the swing arm and corrosion on the fork lowers.

Give your bike a proper wash with motorcycle-specific cleaner. Get into all the nooks—under the tank, around the engine, inside the mudguards. Dry it thoroughly. And I mean thoroughly. Use an air line if you've got one, or a leaf blower works surprisingly well for getting water out of awkward spots.

Once it's clean and dry, apply ACF-50 or similar corrosion protection. I cover everything except brake discs and pads. It's messy work, but after a winter stored, you'll pull the cover off to a bike that looks like you parked it yesterday.

Fuel System Preparation

Here's where people get confused, and I've heard every piece of contradictory advice going. My approach, after storing bikes for fifteen winters: fill the tank completely with fresh fuel and add a fuel stabiliser.

Why fill it? Because an empty or half-full tank allows condensation to form inside, which leads to rust. A full tank minimises the air space and prevents this. Modern ethanol fuel goes off after a few months, hence the stabiliser.

Run the engine for five minutes after adding stabiliser to get it through the fuel system. Then here's the crucial bit: if you're storing for more than two months, I'd recommend draining the carburettors if you've got them. Fuel injection bikes are generally fine with stabiliser alone.

You can pick up fuel stabiliser from SportsBikeShop along with most of your other storage essentials—they've got a decent range of maintenance products that actually work.

Battery Care—Don't Skip This

Dead batteries are the number one reason bikes won't start after storage. Even a new battery will discharge over a few months, and a completely flat battery can suffer permanent damage, especially in cold temperatures.

You've got two options: remove the battery and keep it indoors on a trickle charger, or leave it in and connect a smart charger. I prefer the latter for convenience—modern smart chargers monitor and maintain the battery without overcharging.

If you're removing it, store it somewhere cool but not freezing. A shelf in your house is fine. Put it on a trickle charger once a month for 24 hours. Never let it completely discharge.

For bikes with lots of electronics (looking at you, modern adventure bikes), I've found that disconnecting the negative terminal even with a trickle charger helps prevent phantom drain from alarm systems and clocks.

Tyres and Suspension

Tyres develop flat spots if they sit in one position for months supporting the bike's weight. The longer they sit, the worse it gets. I've got a few strategies:

  • Ideal: get the bike on paddock stands so both wheels are off the ground
  • Good: get at least the rear wheel up on a stand
  • Acceptable: slightly over-inflate the tyres (add 5-10 psi) and rotate the bike every few weeks

If you're storing outside or in a damp garage, flat spots are more likely because of temperature fluctuations. Another reason to get those wheels off the ground if you can.

For suspension, I don't bother with anything special for a standard winter storage. Some people say to release fork pressure by removing weight from the front end, but unless you're storing for six months plus, I've never had an issue.

Oil and Filter Changes

There's debate about this one. Some say change before storage, others say after. I'm firmly in the "before storage" camp, and here's why: used oil contains acids and contaminants from combustion. Leave that sitting in your engine for months and it can cause corrosion on internal surfaces.

Fresh oil before storage means your engine's internals are coated in clean, protective lubricant all winter. Yes, you might want to change it again in spring if you're the belt-and-braces type, but at minimum, go into storage with fresh oil.

While you're at it, change the filter too. It's cheap insurance. I always buy my filters and oil in bulk when there's an offer on—makes these jobs less painful to the wallet.

Protecting Your Bike's Finish

After all that cleaning and ACF-50 application, you want to keep your bike in good nick. Here's my system:

Breathable Cover

Get a proper motorcycle cover, not a tarp. It needs to breathe to prevent condensation buildup. I use one with soft lining so it doesn't scratch the paintwork. Make sure it's actually designed for motorcycles—car covers don't fit right and can do more harm than good.

Chrome and Metal Protection

If you've got chrome exhausts, wrap them in oiled rags or apply a good layer of protective spray. British winters are murder on chrome. My Street Triple's headers looked perfect after winter storage because I took ten minutes to wrap them properly.

Rubber and Plastic

Apply a UV protectant to plastic panels and rubber seals. This isn't just for looks—UV damage happens even in storage if there's any natural light, and rubber can dry out in cold conditions.

The Little Things That Matter

Here's a bunch of smaller jobs that take minutes but save headaches:

  • Stuff the exhaust outlets with oily rags or plastic bags to keep moisture and vermin out (yes, mice love exhausts as winter homes)
  • Remove any luggage or accessories that might trap moisture
  • Put the bike in gear and leave the handbrake off (cable can seize)
  • Spray brake and gear levers with WD-40 or similar—prevents seized pivots
  • If you've got a chain, clean and lube it properly before storage
  • Leave a note on the bike with the storage date and what you did—you'll forget by March

I also put a container of silica gel crystals near the bike if storing in a garage. They absorb moisture from the air. You can dry them out in the oven and reuse them—costs nothing and genuinely helps.

The single biggest mistake I see with winter storage is people thinking a cover alone is enough. Proper storage is about protecting every system on your bike, from fuel to battery to metalwork. Do it right once, and you'll save yourself days of recommissioning work.

Monthly Check-Ins

If possible, check on your bike once a month. I know it's tempting to forget about it until spring, but a quick visit lets you spot any problems early.

What I check:

  • Battery voltage (should hold above 12.4V with a smart charger)
  • No obvious leaks or moisture accumulation
  • Cover's still secure and not torn
  • No signs of vermin (look for droppings or nesting materials)
  • Tyre pressures haven't dropped significantly

Some people start their bikes monthly. I don't. Short runs without properly warming the engine cause more harm than good—you get condensation in the exhaust and oil without burning it off. If you're going to run it, take it for a proper 20-minute ride, which rather defeats the point of storage.

Insurance Considerations

Quick note on this: tell your insurer if you're storing your bike off-road. Some policies let you switch to "laid up" cover which is cheaper and still protects against theft and fire. If you cancel completely and someone nicks it from your garage, you're stuffed.

Also check your garage or storage unit insurance actually covers motorcycles—some household policies exclude them or limit the value.

Planning Your Spring Recommissioning

Before you think about that first spring ride up to the Island to Highlands route, you need to wake your bike up properly. I always set aside a weekend in late March to do this right.

Your recommissioning checklist should include:

  • Full visual inspection for any winter damage or corrosion
  • Check all fluid levels and condition
  • Remove exhaust plugs and any storage rags (don't laugh—I nearly started a bike with rags still in once)
  • Inspect tyres for any deterioration or flat spots
  • Check brake fluid and brake function
  • Verify lights, indicators, and horn all work
  • Reset tyre pressures to normal
  • Check chain tension and condition

Start the bike and let it warm up fully. Listen for anything unusual. Check for leaks. Take it for a gentle test ride—don't head straight for the twisties until you're confident everything's working as it should.

Is Year-Round Riding Better?

Controversial take: if you can ride year-round, your bike will probably stay in better condition than if you store it. Regular use keeps everything moving, prevents seized components, and you spot problems immediately.

But that's only true if you're actually riding regularly and washing off road salt after winter rides. A bike that sits outside for three months covered in salt while you "meant to ride it" would be better off stored properly.

I split the difference—I've got a winter hack for salty days and keep my touring bike stored for the worst months. When I pull it out in spring, it's ready for those first sunny rides without needing major recommissioning work.

Your Storage Action Plan

Right, here's how to actually do this. Pick a dry weekend in late November or early December before the really grim weather sets in:

Day One Morning: Deep clean the bike. Properly. Every inch. Dry it thoroughly.

Day One Afternoon: Change oil and filter while everything's accessible. Apply corrosion protection to all metal surfaces.

Day Two Morning: Deal with fuel—fill tank, add stabiliser, run engine. Sort the battery situation. Get tyres off the ground if possible.

Day Two Afternoon: All the finishing touches—protect chrome, stuff exhausts, apply cover, make notes on what you did.

Total time: maybe 4-6 hours depending on how thorough you are. Seems like a lot? Compare it to the time you'd spend in spring dealing with corrosion, seized parts, and a bike that won't start. I'll take the storage prep every time.

Use the trip planning tool to map out those first spring routes now—gives you something to look forward to while the bike's sleeping. I'm already planning a Scotland run for when the weather breaks.

Final Thoughts

Look, I get that winter storage feels like admitting defeat. We all want to be those hardy souls riding through snow and ice. But there's no shame in protecting your investment and making sure your bike's in perfect condition when riding's actually enjoyable again.

The difference between bikes that last twenty years looking great and those that look tired after five often comes down to winter care. Spend a few hours now sorting proper storage, and you won't be that person in the cafe in April complaining about corroded brake calipers and a battery that won't hold charge.

Next time I'm putting my bike away, I'll probably still feel a bit sad about it. But I'll also know that when I pull that cover off in March, I'll be turning the key on a bike that's ready to go, not one that needs a week of fixing first. That makes the effort worthwhile every time.
